subject: Architecture
title: Water Waste in Buildings
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Water Waste in Buildings.

hook.text: A typical office building wastes 30% of the water it uses. Most of it goes straight down the drain.

buildup.text: Toilets, cooling towers, and irrigation consume vast amounts of treated drinking water unnecessarily.

discovery.text: Rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling can cut a building's water consumption in half.

twist.text: Singapore's Marina Bay Sands collects rainwater from its rooftop pool deck to supply its cooling systems.

climax.text: The Living Building Challenge requires buildings to generate all their own water — a radical standard.

punchline.text: We flush toilets with drinking water. Architecture can fix that.

quiz.question: How much water does a typical office building waste?

details.summary: Buildings consume roughly 12% of all freshwater globally, with inefficient fixtures, leaks, and cooling systems wasting enormous volumes. Low-flow fixtures, rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling.
details.whyItMatters: As freshwater scarcity intensifies globally, buildings that waste water become increasingly untenable. Architecture must treat water as the precious finite resource it is, designing buildings that minimize consumption and maximize reuse.
takeaways: Buildings consume roughly 12% of all freshwater globally
Low-flow fixtures and recycling cut water use by 40-60%
Rainwater harvesting and greywater reuse reduce demand further

faq.question: What is greywater recycling?
faq.answer: Greywater is wastewater from sinks, showers, and washing machines — not toilets. It can be filtered and reused for toilet flushing, irrigation, and cooling tower makeup water. A typical greywater system can reduce a building's potable water demand by 30-40% with relatively simple treatment.

faq.question: How much water does rainwater harvesting save?
faq.answer: A 200-square-meter roof in a city with 800mm annual rainfall can collect about 128,000 liters per year — enough for toilet flushing and irrigation for a typical household. In commercial buildings, larger roofs can offset substantial portions of non-potable water demand.
